headline: 36 years of waiting: Scotland bag first World Cup win since 1990
summary: A deflected strike from John McGinn secured a 1-0 victory over Haiti, putting Scotland at the top of Group C.
details: Scotland ended a 36-year drought by defeating Haiti 1-0 on Saturday, marking their first victory in the World Cup since 1990.
The decisive goal came in the 28th minute when John McGinn's shot took a double deflection and landed in the back of the net.
Scotland nearly scored earlier through Scott McTominay, whose effort hit the post, while Haiti struggled with clinical finishing despite their pace.
This win puts Scotland at the top of World Cup Group C. Haiti, making their first appearance since 1974, now faces a tough challenge ahead.
Scotland is scheduled to play Morocco on June 19, while Haiti will face the five-time world champions on the same day.
caption:
First win in 36 years! Scotland finally breaks the World Cup curse with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Haiti.

Scotland ended a 36-year drought by defeating Haiti 1-0 on Saturday, marking their first victory in the World Cup since 1990.

The decisive goal came in the 28th minute when John McGinn's shot took a double deflection and landed in the back of the net.

Scotland nearly scored earlier through Scott McTominay, whose effort hit the post, while Haiti struggled with clinical finishing despite their pace.

This win puts Scotland at the top of World Cup Group C. Haiti, making their first appearance since 1974, now faces a tough challenge ahead.

Scotland is scheduled to play Morocco on June 19, while Haiti will face the five-time world champions on the same day.

headline_marked: Switzerland votes to [[cap population at 10 million]] by 2050
headline: Switzerland votes to cap population at 10 million by 2050
summary: A high-stakes referendum could trigger restrictions on immigration and jeopardize Switzerland's free movement of labor agreement with the European Union.
details: Swiss voters are deciding in a national referendum whether to limit the country's population to 10 million people by the year 2050. The proposal, pushed by the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP), comes amid growing concerns over immigration and pressure on housing and public services.
Official projections suggest Switzerland is currently on track to hit the 10 million mark by the early 2040s. The country's population is already above 9 million, with an aging demographic.

If the cap is adopted, reaching the limit would trigger a process that could lead Switzerland to scrap its free movement of labor agreement with the EU. This agreement is vital as EU member states provide a significant portion of the Swiss workforce.

The Swiss government and parliament have urged citizens to reject the initiative, calling it 'folly' that could damage the export-oriented economy. They warn it could complicate corporate planning and trade relations with Brussels.

Supporters of the cap argue that economic prosperity has not kept pace with the rate of immigration. They believe the government must 'step on the brakes' to prevent overcrowding from stretching infrastructure to its limit.

Under Switzerland's system of direct democracy, national referendums are held several times a year. For this proposal to pass, it requires the support of both the majority of voters and the majority of the cantons.
